The five essential temples on Koh Samui are Big Buddha (Wat Phra Yai) and Wat Plai Laem in the north-east, Wat Khunaram with its mummified monk and the carved Red Temple (Wat Sila Ngu) in the south-east, and the gold seafront chedi at Laem Sor on the south coast. All are free and mostly open from about 07:00 to 17:00–18:30. Cover shoulders and knees, take your shoes off inside the halls, and see the north-east pair and the southern group as two easy half days.

Map of Koh Samui's temples and shrines

The map shows every temple, Chinese shrine and hilltop chedi in this guide, plus the mosque at Hua Thanon. The busy sights cluster in two places: the north-east tip near the airport (Big Buddha, Wat Plai Laem, Khao Hua Jook) and the south-east between Lamai and Na Mueang (Red Temple, Guan Yu, Wat Khunaram). Laem Sor and the Chinese Temple of Guanyin sit on the quieter south and south-west coasts.

Hours are those checked in November 2026; temples can close halls for ceremonies, and hours shift on Buddhist holidays. None of the temples charges entry; the Secret Buddha Garden is a private sculpture garden, which is why it has a fee.

The best Koh Samui temples to visit

Big Buddha (Wat Phra Yai)

The golden seated Buddha on Koh Fan, a small islet joined by a causeway to the north-east coast about 3 km from the airport, is the island's best-known sight. Entry is free and it is open 07:00–18:30. A naga staircase climbs to the platform, where you walk barefoot around the statue with views over Bang Rak bay to Koh Phangan. Height figures of 12 m and 15 m both circulate and we haven't found an official one, so we don't quote it. Go before 09:30, when the tour vans arrive, or in the late afternoon. It is also one of the two main places on Samui to float a krathong at Loy Krathong. Full guide: Big Buddha, Koh Samui.

Wat Plai Laem

About 1 km east of Big Buddha, Wat Plai Laem is a colourful Thai-Chinese temple built between 2004 and 2009 on a lake. A white 18-armed Guanyin, the bodhisattva of compassion, stands on one platform; a big, round, laughing Phra Sangkachai sits on another; the tiled ordination hall seems to float between them. Feeding the catfish and turtles with temple-sold food is a form of merit-making that children love. Free, about 06:00–18:00, 30–45 minutes. Full guide: Wat Plai Laem.

Wat Khunaram: the mummified monk

On the ring road in Na Mueang, Wat Khunaram displays the body of Luang Pho Daeng (1894–1973), a Samui-born meditation teacher who married, raised six children, became a monk again at about 50 and died seated in meditation in 1973. At his request, his body sits upright in a glass case as a lesson in impermanence. It is a working temple: dress modestly, keep your voice low and photograph respectfully, without flash. Free, daylight hours, 20–30 minutes. Full guide: Wat Khunaram.

The Red Temple: Wat Ratchathammaram (Wat Sila Ngu)

Two kilometres south of central Lamai on the ring road, the Red Temple's hall is deep terracotta red from roof to floor and covered in carved reliefs: guardians, sea creatures, garudas and figures from Buddhist and Hindu stories. It is a modern building, unlike anything else on the island. Open 07:00–17:00, free; go early, when low light brings out the carving. Full guide: the Red Temple.

Laem Sor Pagoda and Khao Chedi

A gold-tiled chedi (yellow-glazed tiles, not real gold) on a rocky outcrop at the end of Bang Kao beach. The first chedi on the site dates from about 1907 and was built of coral stone on a hill; after lightning damaged it in 1967, the seaside chedi was built and the relics moved into it. A white chedi on the hill to the west, Khao Chedi, rewards a short, steep climb with views to Koh Tan. Open 07:00–18:00, free; best in the late afternoon, and rarely crowded. Full guide: Laem Sor Pagoda.

Guan Yu Shrine

A 16 m bronze statue of Guan Yu, the deified Chinese general of loyalty and righteousness, rises above Hua Thanon on the inland side of the ring road. The shrine was built by Samui's Chinese-descended community in the mid-2010s and is one of the focal points of Chinese New Year. Free, about 08:00–17:00, 30 minutes. Full guide: Guan Yu Shrine.

Chinese Temple of Guanyin, Taling Ngam

A small, quiet Chinese temple dedicated to Guanyin on the south-west coast near Taling Ngam (GPS about 9.4212, 99.9479). It sees few visitors and makes a peaceful stop on the way to a sunset at Taling Ngam beach. Open in daylight; no fee is published, so bring small notes for a donation.

Wat Samret

A village temple on the Na Mueang road in the south of the island (GPS about 9.4380, 100.0106), visited mostly by locals. It is described as one of Samui's older temples, said to be over 150 years old. [check] Expect a working temple, not a showpiece; come for an unhurried look at village temple life.

Wat Namtok Hin Lad

The forest temple at the start of the Hin Lad waterfall trail, about 2 km south of Nathon. Forest temples are places of meditation; walk through quietly, dress modestly even if you are going on to hike, and don't swim or picnic in the temple grounds. The trail beyond is steep and uneven; allow about two hours for the round trip.

Khao Hua Jook Chedi

A hilltop chedi above Chaweng (GPS about 9.5371, 100.0589) with a view over Chaweng Lake, the beach and the airport. The access road is steep; scooter riders need experience and good brakes. Come for sunrise or late afternoon, and treat it as a temple rather than just a viewpoint: shoes off at the chedi, no climbing on it.

Pra Buddha Dipankara

A Buddha image in the hills of Na Mueang (GPS about 9.5020, 100.0060), reached by steep interior roads. It is not on standard tours and we are still checking its access, hours and facilities, so treat it as one for confident drivers who like exploring. [check]

Secret Buddha Garden (a sculpture garden, not a temple)

Also called Tarnim Magic Garden, this hilltop garden of Buddhist and folk sculptures was begun in 1976 by its local creator and opened to visitors after his death in 1990. Entry is 80–100 THB (sources differ) and it is open 09:00–18:00. The road is very steep: go by 4x4 or on a tour, not on a rental scooter. Full guide: Secret Buddha Garden.

What you're looking at: a quick guide to Thai temple buildings

A Thai wat is a whole compound, not a single building, and knowing its parts makes any visit more interesting. Most Samui temples have some or all of the following.

  • Ubosot (bot), the ordination hall: the most sacred building, where monks are ordained. You can recognise it by the eight boundary stones (bai sema), shaped like leaves, set around it at the corners and sides. At Wat Plai Laem it is the tiled hall that seems to float on the lake.
  • Viharn (wihan), the assembly hall: where lay people gather to pray and listen to monks, usually with the main Buddha image at the far end. The Red Temple's carved hall is a viharn.
  • Chedi: a bell-shaped or tapering tower that holds relics of the Buddha, a revered monk or a family's ashes. Laem Sor's gold-tiled tower and Khao Hua Jook above Chaweng are chedis.
  • Sala: an open-sided pavilion for resting, meetings and merit-making meals.
  • Kuti: the monks' living quarters, usually at the back of the compound. Don't wander in.
  • Chofa: the slender, horn-like finials at the ends of the roof ridges, often read as a stylised garuda or naga head.
  • Naga: the serpent guardians that run down staircases and roof edges, as at Big Buddha's staircase. In Buddhist legend a naga king sheltered the meditating Buddha from a storm.
  • Yak: giant guardian figures with swords or clubs at gates and doors, as at Laem Sor.
  • Garuda: the bird-man of Hindu-Buddhist myth and the royal emblem of Thailand, often seen supporting roofs.
  • Buddha postures: the seated "calling the earth to witness" pose (right hand reaching to the ground) is the most common. Thai temples often have a line of smaller images showing the posture for each day of the week; Thais make offerings at the image for the day they were born.

Chinese shrines follow a different plan: an entrance gate, an incense urn in a courtyard, and a main hall with the principal deity at the back and secondary altars to the sides. Red stands for luck and protection, and you will often see paper offerings burned in a separate furnace.

Chinese shrines and Samui's Hainanese heritage

Many of Samui's merchant families descend from Chinese settlers, especially from Hainan Island, who traded coconuts and goods long before tourism arrived. Their shrines are smaller than the big Buddhist temples but are where the island's Chinese festivals happen.

  • Hainan Shrine, Nathon: the traditional heart of the Hainanese community in the old port town. Its Chinese New Year rites are the most traditional on the island and have included face-piercing rituals that may not suit children.
  • San Chao Jao Eng Sae, Maenam: the Chinese temple in Maenam's small Chinatown, with lion and dragon dances at Chinese New Year; the most family-friendly celebration.
  • Guan Yu Shrine, Hua Thanon: the newest and largest, with its 16 m bronze statue (see above).
  • Chinese Temple of Guanyin, Taling Ngam: quiet, off the main circuit.

Chinese New Year 2027 falls on Saturday 6 February 2027. Expect red lanterns, firecrackers, offerings and lion dances over several days; the island programme is usually confirmed in January. See Chinese New Year on Koh Samui. At Chinese shrines, offer incense with both hands and bow three times, never blow incense out, and don't bring beef as an offering.

The mosque at Hua Thanon

Hua Thanon, on the south-east coast just past Lamai, is a Muslim fishing village with Koh Samui's central mosque, Masjid Nurul Ihsan, built in 1984. It is a place of worship, not a tourist sight, but the village and its morning fish market are worth a visit. If you want to look inside the mosque, ask first, avoid the five daily prayer times (which change with the sun) and Friday midday prayers, dress conservatively (long sleeves and long trousers or skirt; women should cover their hair), take your shoes off and speak quietly. Photograph people only with permission. More on the village: Hua Thanon.

Temple etiquette and dress code

What to wear

  • Shoulders and knees covered at every temple and shrine: T-shirt or blouse with sleeves, trousers, long shorts below the knee or a long skirt.
  • No beachwear: no bikinis, vests, crop tops or swim shorts. Big Buddha turns away visitors who aren't covered.
  • Carry a sarong. Some temples lend wraps and some sell them; many do neither. A sarong in your day bag solves every situation.
  • Slip-on shoes save time; you take them off before entering halls and on some platforms.

How to behave

  • Feet: never point your feet at a Buddha image, a monk or a shrine. When you sit, tuck your feet behind you or to the side.
  • Head: don't touch anyone's head, including children's; the head is considered the highest part of the body.
  • Buddha images: never climb on, sit on or lean against them, and don't pose disrespectfully (for example with your back to the image and arms raised, or pretending to hold it). Buddha images are protected by Thai law, and Buddha-head tattoos and souvenirs are seen as disrespectful.
  • Direction: walk clockwise around chedis and statues.
  • Thresholds: step over the raised threshold at a hall door, not on it.
  • Voices and phones: keep both low; switch off your ringer.
  • Drones: don't fly them over temples without permission.

Monks and women

Monks may not touch women or take things directly from a woman's hand. Women should not touch a monk, sit right next to one or hand anything to him directly; place it on a cloth or table in front of him, or ask a man to pass it. On songthaews and in waiting areas, leave the seat next to a monk free. Men can hand things to monks directly, with both hands or the right hand supported by the left. Women can of course visit every temple in this guide and can talk to monks, keeping a respectful distance.

Making merit and donations

  • Donation boxes: 20–100 THB is a normal gift at a free temple.
  • Offerings: flowers, candles and incense are sold at most temples. Gold leaf is pressed onto Buddha images; follow what local people do.
  • Fortune sticks (siam si): shake a cylinder of numbered sticks until one falls, then read the matching slip. You'll find this at Wat Plai Laem.
  • Alms round: monks walk through villages at dawn collecting food. If you want to give, buy a prepared alms set, kneel or stand lower than the monk, place the food in the bowl without touching him, and don't chase the procession with a camera.
  • Feeding fish: only with food sold by the temple.

Photos at Samui temples

Outdoor photos are welcome at every temple in this guide. Indoors, follow the signs: some halls ban photos, and where they are allowed, turn off flash and the shutter sound. Never photograph monks or worshippers at close range without asking, and don't use a Buddha image as a backdrop for selfies or posed shots. At Wat Khunaram, respectful photos of the mummified monk are generally tolerated, but no selfies beside the case. Drones need permission. Good light: Big Buddha and Wat Plai Laem early morning; the Red Temple 07:00–09:30; Laem Sor late afternoon.

Buddhist holidays follow the lunar calendar, so dates marked provisional can move by a day; we update this table as the official calendar is published. On the big holy days, temples are busy with local families from early evening. Visitors are welcome to watch the candle processions; if you join, walk quietly with the line and hold the candle, flowers and incense you are given.

Alcohol-ban days and what stays open

On Makha Bucha, Visakha Bucha, Asahna Bucha, Khao Phansa and Ok Phansa, Thailand bans alcohol sales nationwide. Since May 2025, hotels, licensed entertainment venues and licensed bars in tourist areas may still serve on these days, so most beach clubs and bars in Chaweng carry on. Shops, 7-Eleven and unlicensed restaurants can't sell. The next ban day after this guide's update is Sunday 21 February 2027 (Makha Bucha). There are no ban days in November or December 2026, and Loy Krathong, Songkran and Chinese New Year are not ban days. Normal sales hours are 11:00–24:00 since 29 May 2026, and alcohol is never sold at temples. Details: Koh Samui drugs and alcohol law.

Meditation and temple life

Several of Samui's temples are working monasteries where monks study and meditate; Wat Namtok Hin Lad in particular is a forest temple. Most don't run drop-in classes for visitors, but you can sit quietly in a hall at any temple for a few minutes, and monks are often happy to talk if you approach respectfully. For structured practice, the island has meditation centres and retreats with fixed schedules, from evening sits to multi-day silent retreats; book these ahead. See meditation on Koh Samui, retreats and Thai culture and traditions for how to approach monks, alms giving and temple customs.

Two half-day temple routes

North-east route (about 3 hours)

  1. 07:30 Big Buddha, before the tour vans (free, 07:00–18:30)
  2. 08:30 Wat Plai Laem, about 1 km east; feed the fish
  3. 09:30 Khao Hua Jook Chedi above Chaweng for the view (steep road)
  4. 10:30 Swim at Choeng Mon or coffee in Fisherman's Village

South route (about 4 hours)

  1. 08:00 Hin Ta and Hin Yai, south end of Lamai (free, parking about 30 THB)
  2. 08:45 Red Temple, in the best morning light
  3. 09:30 Guan Yu Shrine and the Hua Thanon fish market
  4. 10:30 Wat Khunaram and the mummified monk
  5. 11:30 Laem Sor Pagoda, then lunch in Bang Kao or Thong Krut
  6. Afternoon Pig Island from Thong Krut, or a sunset at Taling Ngam

Both routes fit a scooter or a hired car with driver (a full-day taxi is about 2,000–3,000 THB). Shared 4x4 jungle safaris cover Big Buddha, Wat Khunaram, Na Muang waterfall and the Secret Buddha Garden in one day (market price about 1,700 THB); enquire on our jungle safari page.

Times are without traffic. Grab works well in the north and east but cars are scarce in the south and west, so plan your return. Taxis don't use meters; agree the price first. Songthaews run along the ring road in daytime (locals pay about 30–80 THB; most stop by 20:00–22:00). If you ride a scooter, you need an International Driving Permit with the motorcycle category, and the helmet fine is up to 2,000 THB. Route 4170 in the south-west is steep and slippery when wet. More: getting around Koh Samui.

Seasonal and safety notes

Temples are open all year, which makes them one of the best things to do in the north-east monsoon (October to December), when November is the wettest month with about 445 mm of rain. Plan short visits between showers and watch for slippery tiles and steps. February to April is the driest and calmest period; April and May are the hottest (highs of 32–33 °C), when platforms and courtyards burn bare feet by midday, so go early. Carry water, sun protection and small change for donations and parking. Emergency numbers: Tourist Police 1155, ambulance 1669.

Add a boat trip to your stay

Ang Thong Marine Park is closed every year from 1 November to 15 December and reopens on 16 December. Pig Island runs every day of the year and pairs well with the south route, since boats leave from Thong Krut near Laem Sor.
